title: Cross-company yield and quality data exchange: foundry and OSAT to chip designers and their customers
why_it_matters: A fabless company does not own its fab or test floor, so everything it knows about how its chips are coming out depends on what the foundry and packaging houses choose to send back. The only evidence so far that defect and metrology data are withheld is one vendor blog [CLM-0451].
questions: Which manufacturing data types (WAT/PCM, sort maps, bin summaries, inline defect, metrology, FDC excursions, final test) do foundries and OSATs share with customers, and which do they withhold?

Through which channels (TSMC-Online/TSMC-Direct, UMC/GlobalFoundries/Samsung portals, OSAT portals, B2B links, file drops) and in which formats (STDF, SEMI E142, CSV) is the data delivered, and how often?
How does data sharing differ for automotive and other safety-critical customers (e.g. under AEC-Q100/Q001 part average testing, IATF 16949 obligations)?
What do contracts or published terms say about data ownership and confidentiality of manufacturing data?
Which third-party platforms (e.g. PDF Solutions Exensio, yieldHUB, Synopsys SLM, proteanTecs) aggregate cross-company data, and what do they claim about access?
subquestions: Is there a published foundry data-sharing policy or service description per foundry?
Do customers pay separately for extended data access?
How long is the data retained and by whom (link to CLM-0452)?

AEC-Q001 (part average testing) and AEC-Q004 (zero-defects guideline) documents
SEMI E142 and STDF V4 specifications

title: Known-good-die, HBM and chiplet test-data exchange across memory makers, foundries and OSATs
why_it_matters: AI chips now combine dies from several companies (logic, HBM stacks, interposers) in one package. If one die is bad, the whole expensive package is lost, so test data must cross company lines. imec names known-good-die testing as a key chiplet challenge [CLM-0434] but how the data actually flows is unknown (INT-0017).
questions: What test coverage and data does an HBM supplier (SK hynix, Samsung, Micron) deliver with each stack to the package integrator?
How do CoWoS-class integrators (TSMC, and OSATs such as ASE/SPIL and Amkor) combine test data from different die suppliers?
Which standards govern die-level traceability and test data in multi-die packages (IEEE 1838, UCIe test/repair, JEDEC HBM4 test features, SEMI E142 extensions)?
When a multi-die package fails, how is the failing die attributed and who bears the cost?
Which parties hold the combined genealogy (die ID to package ID)?
subquestions: Is die-level electronic chip ID (ECID) data shared across companies?
Do contracts specify KGD yield guarantees?

title: Product change, end-of-life and compliance information sent to chip customers (PCN/PDN, material declarations)
why_it_matters: Customers such as carmakers design a chip into products that last 10-20 years. When a supplier changes a process, fab or package, or discontinues a part, the notice triggers requalification or last-time buys. These notices and material declarations are a core, largely document-based information flow.

questions: What steps does a fab take to qualify a new supplier or grade (sample evaluation, pilot lots, reliability, customer notification)?
How long does it take for photoresist, HF/wet chemicals, specialty gases, wafers, substrates?
What change-control obligations exist toward customers (PCNs, automotive requirements)?
What did Korean firms do in 2019-2020 to localise HF, photoresist and polyimide, and how long did it take?
How did firms respond to the 2022 neon disruption?
subquestions: What SEMI standards (e.g. SEMI C-series material specs) support multi-sourcing?

title: Leading indicators and high-frequency datasets for the semiconductor cycle
why_it_matters: The industry swings sharply. Several public monthly series (sales, equipment billings, exports, company revenues) can show where the cycle is, but each measures something different. The atlas needs a catalogue of them, with coverage, lag and caveats.
questions: What does each series measure, how often, with what lag and access: WSTS/SIA monthly sales, SEMI equipment billings (North America, worldwide), SEAJ Japanese equipment billings, Korea Customs Service semiconductor exports (including 10-day data), Taiwan MOF export statistics and MOEA export orders, TWSE monthly revenue reports (MOPS), Japan METI production statistics, China NBS monthly IC output, US Federal Reserve industrial production for semiconductors (G.17), US Census M3?
How well did these series lead or coincide with the 2019, 2021-22 and 2023 turning points?
Which price series exist (US BLS PPI for semiconductors, Japan BOJ CGPI, DRAM/NAND spot and contract indices)?
Which are free vs paid?
subquestions: Which series have been discontinued or redefined (e.g. SEMI book-to-bill)?
primary_sources: Taiwan MOF trade statistics and MOEA export orders
TWSE Market Observation Post System (MOPS) monthly revenue
Federal Reserve G.17 industrial production series for semiconductors (FRED IPG3344S, to verify series ID)
China NBS monthly industrial output (integrated circuits)
BLS PPI semiconductor series (to verify series ID)

title: Company disclosure systems by jurisdiction: what chip companies must publish and where (EDGAR, MOPS, DART, EDINET/TDnet, HKEX, SSE/SZSE, Euronext, TASE, NSE/BSE)
why_it_matters: Most company facts in the atlas must come from filings. Each jurisdiction's filing system has different content (segment data, monthly revenue in Taiwan, related-party disclosures in China), and researchers need to know where to look.
questions: Which filing systems hold semiconductor companies' reports in the US, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, China (mainland, incl. STAR Market), Hong Kong, the Netherlands/EU, Israel and India?
What does each require: annual/quarterly reports, monthly revenue (Taiwan), segment and customer-concentration disclosure, capacity or capex disclosure?
Which languages, formats (XBRL, PDF) and APIs are available?
How can these systems be used to enumerate listed companies by industry code (SIC 3674, TWSE semiconductor sector, KRX industry codes, CSRC classification)?
What is typically NOT disclosed (e.g. wafer prices, customer names)?
subquestions: Which major private companies (e.g. Kioxia before IPO, CXMT, YMTC) disclose via bond prospectuses or IPO filings?
primary_sources: SEC EDGAR full-text search and SIC code 3674 listing
Japan FSA EDINET and JPX TDnet
secondary_sources: Guides by academic libraries to international filings
open_questions: Supports company-discovery units owned by the participants/competition planners.

title: Trade statistics for chips and chipmaking tools: datasets, mirror discrepancies and transshipment
why_it_matters: Trade data are the main official record of where chips and tools move, but they record where goods cross borders, not where chips were designed or made, and packaging and transshipment distort them [CLM-0010]. They are also used to spot export-control diversion.
questions: Which datasets report HS 8541, 8542 and 8486 trade and at what detail (UN Comtrade, USITC DataWeb, Eurostat Comext, China Customs, Taiwan MOF, Korea KITA/KCS, Japan MOF, Malaysia DOSM, Singapore)?
How large are mirror discrepancies (exporter vs importer reports), and why (Hong Kong re-exports, valuation, processing trade)?
What do trade data show about China's imports of chipmaking tools 2022-2026 around export-control changes?
How are chips counted when embedded in finished goods (value-added trade: OECD TiVA)?
What trade data evidence exists of diversion of controlled items via third countries?
subquestions: What national-level HS extensions exist (e.g. US HTS 10-digit for 8542.31)?
primary_sources: China General Administration of Customs statistics
WCO HS 2022 nomenclature notes for chapters 85 and 84
secondary_sources: CSET and Rhodium analyses of trade data (to verify)
Academic work on semiconductor mirror statistics

title: Fab and capacity datasets: coverage and reliability of fab-level databases
why_it_matters: Capacity statistics by region and node come from a few fab databases, mostly paid. The atlas must know which public sources can be used to count fabs and capacity and how they differ.
questions: Which fab-level databases exist (SEMI World Fab Forecast, Knometa Research, TechInsights, CSET, SIA/BCG), what do they cover, and what is public?
How is capacity measured (wafer starts per month, 200mm-equivalent), and how do sources differ?
Which government sources list fabs (e.g. Taiwan science-park administrations, Japan METI, EU Chips Act pilot-line lists, India ISM approvals, China provincial project lists)?
How reliable are announced-capacity lists vs realised capacity?
primary_sources: SEMI World Fab Forecast public releases
Taiwan Hsinchu/Central/Southern Taiwan Science Park statistics

title: Patent, publication and R&D datasets for semiconductor technology
why_it_matters: Patents and research papers show who is developing which technologies and where. The atlas needs to know which public datasets and classification codes isolate semiconductor technology.
questions: Which CPC classes cover semiconductors (H01L, new H10 scheme from 2023, G03F lithography, G06F design) and how did the 2023 reclassification affect counts?
Which public tools (USPTO PatentsView, EPO Espacenet/PATSTAT, WIPO PATENTSCOPE, CNIPA, Google Patents) can be used, and with what limits?
Which conference datasets (IEDM, ISSCC, VLSI Symposium) track technology leadership?
What public R&D-spending statistics exist (company filings, OECD ANBERD, US NSF BERD)?
primary_sources: CPC scheme H10 (introduced 2023, to verify date)

title: Policy and enforcement datasets: tracking controls, entity lists, subsidies and trade remedies
why_it_matters: Semiconductor rules change monthly. The atlas needs a list of authoritative feeds for rules, entity lists, awards and enforcement actions, so updates can be tracked rather than rediscovered.
questions: Which official feeds publish export-control rules and lists (Federal Register, eCFR, BIS Entity List and Consolidated Screening List API, MOFCOM notices, EU OJ, Netherlands/Japan/Taiwan lists)?
Which sources list subsidy awards (NIST CHIPS awards, EU state-aid register, METI, ISM approvals, China Big Fund investments via company registries)?
Which sources list enforcement actions (BIS penalty orders, DOJ press releases, OFAC)?
Which trade-remedy dockets exist (USTR Section 301 docket, BIS Section 232 docket, MOFCOM trade-remedy cases)?
primary_sources: BIS enforcement 'Penalties and Settlements' page (to verify)

title: The semiconductor business cycle: drivers, inventory dynamics and historical turning points (1985-2026)
why_it_matters: Chip sales rise and fall more than the wider economy (e.g. the 2001 and 2023 falls). Knowing why - long build times, inventory stocking and destocking, capacity additions - is essential before judging any forecast or investment.
questions: What were the dated peaks and troughs of world semiconductor sales since 1985 (WSTS/SIA), and how large were the swings?
What mechanisms drive the cycle (inventory bullwhip, capex lag, memory pricing, end-demand shocks), per academic and official sources?
How do cycles differ between memory, logic, analog and equipment?
Which indicators turned first at each turning point?
Has the cycle changed with fabless/foundry, long-term agreements and AI demand?
subquestions: Is there an academic consensus on cycle length (e.g. 'silicon cycle' ~4 years)?
primary_sources: SIA annual sales releases 2001, 2008, 2022, 2023 (SRC-0055, SRC-0056, SRC-0108)
Federal Reserve / BIS (Bank for International Settlements) or IMF working papers on the semiconductor cycle (to verify)
secondary_sources: Academic papers on the silicon cycle (e.g. Liu 2005, Tan & Mathews, to verify)
open_questions: prereq: Leading indicators and high-frequency datasets

title: The 2020-2023 chip shortage and glut: causes, timeline, who was hit, and how it ended
why_it_matters: The shortage stopped car factories worldwide and triggered chip subsidies in the US, EU and Asia; it was followed by a glut and a 2023 downturn. It is the reference case for supply-chain resilience policy and for current allocation behaviour.
questions: What was the timeline (2020 demand shift, 2021 shortages, 2022 peak lead times, 2022-23 correction)?
What caused it (demand swings, auto order cancellations, fires/storms/drought, COVID lockdowns, double-ordering), per official sources?
Which products and end markets were hit hardest (CLM-0463), and what did it cost (lost vehicle production estimates)?
How did lead times and prices evolve (public lead-time data)?
How did it end and what changed afterwards (inventory targets, LTAs, direct foundry deals by automakers)?
subquestions: Which cost estimates of the shortage are credible and what populations do they cover?
primary_sources: European Commission Chips Act staff working document (2022)
secondary_sources: Industry press on lead times (Susquehanna data as reported)

title: China's semiconductor build-out: localisation, self-sufficiency progress and effects on global markets (2014-2026)
why_it_matters: China is the largest chip-consuming market and is spending heavily to make its own chips and tools under export controls. Its progress changes competition in mature chips, tools and memory worldwide.
questions: What is China's chip self-sufficiency rate by credible estimates, and how is it defined?
How fast is China adding capacity (SMIC, Hua Hong, CXMT, YMTC, Nexchip) and at which nodes?
How far has domestic equipment and materials substitution gone (Naura, AMEC, SMEE, Piotech)?
What evidence exists of advanced-node progress under controls (7nm/5nm-class Huawei/SMIC chips per teardowns)?
How have Chinese firms' import patterns of tools changed 2022-2026?
subquestions: How do Chinese and Western estimates of self-sufficiency differ?
primary_sources: SMIC and Hua Hong annual reports (HKEX/SSE)
USITC paper on Chinese semiconductor industrial policy (SRC-0067)

title: Mature-node (28nm and above) supply, demand and pricing dynamics, including Chinese capacity additions
why_it_matters: Most chips by unit are made on older processes (cars, industrial, power). Rapid capacity additions, largely in China, could depress prices and squeeze non-Chinese producers; the US opened a Section 301 case over it [REG-0016].
questions: How much mature-node capacity exists and is being added, by region?
What has happened to mature-node foundry utilisation and wafer prices 2022-2026 (UMC, GlobalFoundries, Vanguard, Hua Hong disclosures)?
What evidence did USTR and Commerce cite on Chinese legacy chips (Section 301 action, 2024 Commerce legacy-chip survey)?
How are Western mature-node producers (GlobalFoundries, UMC, TI, Infineon) responding?
primary_sources: USTR Section 301 notice of action (SRC-0122) and investigation record
BIS 2024 legacy chip industrial-base survey announcement (to verify)
UMC, GlobalFoundries, VIS, Hua Hong quarterly reports

title: Reshoring and the global fab-building wave: announced vs realised capacity since 2020
why_it_matters: Since 2020 companies have announced hundreds of billions of dollars of new fabs outside Taiwan and Korea. Tracking which are built, delayed or cancelled shows whether the geography of manufacturing is really shifting.
questions: Which major fab projects were announced 2020-2026 in the US, EU, Japan, India, Southeast Asia, and what is each one's status (operating, under construction, delayed, cancelled)?
What reasons were given for delays or cancellations (e.g. Intel Magdeburg and Poland, Intel Ohio timing, Wolfspeed Saarland)?
How do realised capacity shares by 2026 compare with SIA/BCG projections for 2032?
Which projects are tied to subsidies and have milestones?
primary_sources: Company press releases and filings (Intel 10-K, TSMC 20-F, Micron 10-K)
secondary_sources: Industry press trackers of fab projects

title: Capacity investment cycle: capex decisions, fab lead times and utilisation
why_it_matters: Fabs take years to build and are expensive to idle, so capacity decisions made in a boom arrive in a bust. Capex and utilisation data explain much of the cycle and of pricing power.
questions: What is industry capex by year and by segment (foundry, memory, logic IDM) from public sources?
How long from capex decision to output for a new fab vs an expansion?
What utilisation rates have foundries and memory makers disclosed through the cycle?
How do capex cuts and utilisation cuts transmit to equipment makers' orders?
primary_sources: Company capex disclosures (TSMC, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, Intel filings)
SEMI equipment billings and World Fab Forecast public releases
UMC/SMIC utilisation disclosures in quarterly reports

title: Consolidation and M&A dynamics: major deals, blocked deals and merger-review patterns
why_it_matters: The industry has consolidated through big mergers, but many deals have been blocked or abandoned by regulators in China, the US, UK and EU. Merger review is now a strategic constraint on who can combine.
questions: What were the largest semiconductor M&A deals 2015-2026 (e.g. Avago-Broadcom, AMD-Xilinx, Nvidia-Arm (failed), Qualcomm-NXP (failed), Intel-Tower (failed), Synopsys-Ansys)?
Which authorities blocked or conditioned deals and why (China SAMR, US FTC/CFIUS, UK CMA, EU)?
How has consolidation changed concentration in memory, EDA, analog and equipment?
What are current policy positions on semiconductor M&A?
primary_sources: SAMR conditional approval decisions (e.g. Synopsys-Ansys 2025, to verify)

title: Automotive and industrial semiconductor demand dynamics (EVs, SiC/GaN power, content per vehicle, 2024-2026 correction)
why_it_matters: Cars and factories are the second big growth story after AI and were the most hurt by the shortage. Electric vehicles need far more power chips, but the 2024-25 slowdown in EVs and industrial markets hit suppliers such as Infineon, NXP, STMicro and Wolfspeed.
questions: What are the WSTS/SIA automotive and industrial end-use shares and growth rates 2019-2025?
What is semiconductor content per vehicle (ICE vs EV) per public sources?
How did the 2024-2025 auto/industrial downturn show up in supplier results (Infineon, NXP, STMicro, Renesas, TI, onsemi)?
What is happening to SiC and GaN demand and supply (Wolfspeed restructuring, Chinese SiC wafer entrants)?
How did automakers change sourcing after 2021 (direct deals with foundries)?
primary_sources: WSTS end-use survey via SIA Factbook (SRC-0010)
Infineon, NXP, STMicro, Renesas, onsemi annual reports

title: Consumer electronics demand dynamics: smartphones, PCs, and the 'AI PC/phone' refresh
why_it_matters: Smartphones and PCs were long the industry's main demand, and their slump drove the 2022-23 downturn. Whether AI features trigger a refresh cycle matters for memory, mobile SoC and PC-processor makers.
questions: What are smartphone and PC unit shipment trends 2015-2026 (public IDC/Gartner/Canalys releases)?
How much semiconductor value per device, and how is it changing (memory content)?
How did the 2022-23 consumer slump flow into chip inventories and prices?
What evidence exists of an AI-driven refresh?

title: Problems of chip designers (fabless, system companies, start-ups): design cost, respins, access to capacity and tools
why_it_matters: Designing a leading-edge chip keeps getting more expensive, most projects slip, and small firms struggle to get capacity, PDK access and affordable EDA. These pains shape who can enter the industry.
questions: What evidence exists on design-cost escalation by node, and on schedule overruns and respins (Wilson Research Group studies)?
What barriers do start-ups report for access to leading-edge PDKs, MPW slots and foundry capacity (e.g. during 2021 and 2025-26 CoWoS allocation)?
What do EDA and IP costs mean for small teams; what programmes help (open-source PDKs, CHIPS NSTC/Natcast design enablement, EU Chips Act design platform, India's DLI scheme)?
What verification, power and thermal problems dominate at advanced nodes and in chiplet designs?
Which problems are reported by system companies building custom silicon?
primary_sources: Siemens/Wilson Research Group functional verification studies 2024, 2026
NIST CHIPS R&D / NSTC design-enablement documents (to verify post-2025 status)
EU Chips Act design platform (Chips JU) documents
open_questions: prereq: Workflow: chip design from specification to tape-out

title: Problems of chip buyers (OEMs, automotive Tier-1s, EMS): shortages, lead times, obsolescence, qualification lock-in and price volatility
why_it_matters: Chip buyers suffered the most visible pain in 2021: production stoppages and allocation. Obsolescence and long qualification add ongoing costs. Their problems are central to any view of where the industry fails its customers.
questions: What quantified impacts of shortages on OEMs are in filings and official sources (lost production, cost increases, premium payments)?
How often are parts discontinued, and what does obsolescence cost defence, industrial and automotive users (DoD DMSMS programme evidence)?
How does qualification lock-in limit switching?
What problems do buyers report with supplier transparency (lead times, allocation, forecasts; GAO-22-105923)?
How are buyers affected by memory price spikes in 2025-2026?
primary_sources: ECIA or AIAG shortage surveys (to verify)

title: Problems of fab operators (foundries, IDMs, memory makers): yield ramps, utilisation swings, costs, water/power and customer concentration
why_it_matters: Fabs carry the industry's biggest fixed costs. Their pains - slow yield ramps, idle capacity in downturns, high costs outside Asia, resource constraints and dependence on a few customers - decide which fabs survive.
questions: What problems do foundries and IDMs disclose in risk factors (yield, customer concentration, utilisation, input costs)?
What evidence exists on cost differences of operating fabs in the US/EU vs Taiwan (TSMC statements, SIA/BCG)?
How have utilisation swings affected margins (e.g. 2023 mature-node foundries, memory makers' losses)?
What water, power and chemicals constraints are reported (Taiwan 2021 drought, grid reliability)?
Which problems are specific to memory makers (price volatility, HBM yield)?
primary_sources: Samsung and SK hynix business reports (DART)
open_questions: prereq: Workflow: new fab and new process ramp

title: Fab construction and ramp problems outside East Asia: cost, delays, permits, workforce and supply ecosystem
why_it_matters: New US, European, Japanese and Indian fabs are a central policy bet. Reported problems (construction cost, labour shortages, permitting, missing local suppliers) determine whether subsidies deliver.
questions: What delays and cost overruns have been disclosed for TSMC Arizona, Samsung Taylor, Intel Ohio, Micron New York, ESMC Dresden, JASM Kumamoto, Tata Dholera/Micron Sanand?
What causes were cited (labour, permits, NEPA reviews, construction costs, demand, customer commitments)?
What did GAO/CRS/European Court of Auditors find about programme execution?
How does construction time compare across countries (evidence-based)?
primary_sources: European Court of Auditors special report on the Chips Act (2025, to verify)
GAO reports on CHIPS implementation (to verify)
secondary_sources: Industry press; academic work on fab construction times (CSET, to verify)

title: Problems of OSATs and advanced-packaging providers: capacity bottlenecks, substrate shortages, known-good-die and thin margins
why_it_matters: Advanced packaging became the bottleneck for AI chips, and substrates were in acute shortage [CLM-0540]. Conventional OSATs face low margins and customer pressure. These problems sit at the centre of the AI supply chain.
questions: What CoWoS-class capacity bottlenecks were disclosed (TSMC, OSATs) and how long did they last?
What substrate shortages occurred (ABF 2020-2022; glass/cloth shortages 2025-26, to verify) and why?
What margins do OSATs earn vs foundries and how have they changed?
What technical problems (warpage, thermal, KGD, test cost) are reported for 2.5D/3D packaging?
primary_sources: TSMC earnings transcripts on CoWoS (SRC-0023, SRC-0025)

title: Problems of equipment and materials suppliers: export-control revenue loss, lead times, service in restricted markets, customer concentration
why_it_matters: Toolmakers and material suppliers are caught between customers in China and controls at home, and depend on a handful of very large customers. Their pains shape the upstream chokepoints.
questions: What revenue impact from export controls have ASML, Applied Materials, Lam, KLA, TEL disclosed?
What customer-concentration levels are disclosed?
What supply-chain problems did toolmakers report (lead times 2021-22, parts shortages, the 2023 MKS Instruments ransomware incident)?
What problems do materials suppliers report (qualification lock-in, PFAS restrictions, price pressure)?
primary_sources: ASML annual report; Applied, Lam, KLA 10-K; TEL integrated report

title: Problems in the distribution channel: excess inventory, price erosion, counterfeit exposure and disintermediation
why_it_matters: Distributors sit between suppliers and hundreds of thousands of customers and absorb inventory swings; Avnet reported unusually high inventories in the downturn [CLM-0273]. Their pains show where the channel breaks down.
questions: How did distributor inventory and margins move through 2021-2025 (Arrow, Avnet, WPG, WT)?
How do price protection and stock rotation shift risk between supplier and distributor (CLM-0270)?
What threat do suppliers' direct-sales moves pose (e.g. TI's shift away from distribution)?
What problems do brokers face (counterfeits, testing costs, reputational risk)?

title: Counterfeit, recycled and grey-market chips: scale, where they enter, and consequences
why_it_matters: Counterfeit and recycled chips enter through the open market, especially during shortages, and have reached defence systems. SIA advises buying only from manufacturers or authorised distributors [CLM-0545].
questions: What evidence exists on the scale of counterfeiting (SIA estimates, GIDEP/ERAI report counts, US Senate Armed Services 2012 investigation)?
Where do counterfeits enter and which parts are targeted (obsolete parts, shortage parts)?
What legal and procurement rules apply (NDAA 2012 Section 818, DFARS)?
What detection methods and standards exist (SAE AS6171, AS6081)?
primary_sources: US Senate Armed Services Committee report on counterfeit electronic parts (2012, to verify)

title: Silent data corruption and reliability problems in large compute fleets
why_it_matters: Hyperscalers have reported that a small share of processors silently compute wrong answers, which matters more as AI clusters use tens of thousands of chips. It is a test and reliability problem that crosses chip designers, foundries and users.
questions: What have Meta, Google, Alibaba and others published about silent data corruption rates and causes?
What testing responses exist (in-field test, telemetry, OCP initiatives)?
How do GPU/accelerator failure rates in large AI training clusters (e.g. published training-run reports) affect operations?
Who bears the cost?
primary_sources: Meta 'Silent Data Corruptions at Scale' paper (arXiv, 2021, to verify)
Google 'Cores that don't count' (HotOS 2021, to verify)
Open Compute Project SDC initiative materials (to verify)
Meta Llama 3 paper section on training interruptions (to verify)

title: Taiwan concentration and cross-Strait conflict risk: scenarios, exposure and mitigation
why_it_matters: Most of the world's most advanced chips are made in Taiwan. A blockade, conflict or even a prolonged power or shipping disruption would hit every downstream industry. Estimates of the consequences vary widely and need careful sourcing.
questions: What share of leading-edge logic, advanced packaging and foundry capacity is in Taiwan (dated, sourced; CSET, SIA/BCG, USITC SRC-0070)?
What scenarios have credible bodies modelled (blockade, quarantine, conflict), and what economic impacts do they estimate, with methods?
What vulnerabilities besides conflict exist (energy imports ~LNG dependence, grid, shipping and air cargo routes)?
What mitigation is underway (TSMC overseas fabs, customer multi-sourcing, US/Japan policy) and how much would it cover by 2030?
What does Taiwan's government say about 'N-1' rules for overseas nodes (to verify)?
subquestions: How much inventory buffer exists downstream?
primary_sources: USITC working paper 'U.S. Exposure to the Taiwanese Semiconductor Industry' (SRC-0070)
Taiwan MOEA / Bureau of Energy data on energy imports
CSIS wargame reports on Taiwan (2023, to verify)
secondary_sources: Bloomberg Economics scenario estimates as reported

title: Geopolitical weaponisation of chip supply chains: case studies and exposure by participant type (2019-2026)
why_it_matters: Governments have repeatedly cut off chips, tools or materials to put pressure on rivals: Japan-Korea chemicals (2019), Huawei (2019-20), Micron in China (2023), gallium/germanium (2023-25), rare earths (2025) and Nexperia (2025). Each case shows who is exposed and how fast damage spreads.
questions: For each case: what was restricted, by whom, when, what was the measured impact on companies and downstream industries, and how was it resolved?
Which participant types were most exposed in each case (materials suppliers, IDMs, OEMs)?
What does the 2025 Nexperia case show about the vulnerability of legacy chips made or packaged in China for European and US automakers?
What patterns emerge (retaliation lags, workarounds, stockpiling)?
What escalation options remain for the US, China and allies?
primary_sources: CAC Micron decision (to verify official text)
Netherlands Ministry of Economic Affairs statements on Nexperia (Sept-Nov 2025)
MOFCOM notices on Nexperia export restrictions and suspension (Oct-Nov 2025)

title: Geopolitical and conflict risks beyond Taiwan: Korean peninsula, Israel, Russia-Ukraine and Middle East shipping
why_it_matters: Other conflict zones host important chip assets: Korean memory fabs near the DMZ, Intel and Tower fabs in Israel, and Ukrainian neon purifiers [CLM-0533]. Their exposure is less studied than Taiwan's.
questions: What share of memory capacity is within range of North Korea, and what do Samsung/SK hynix disclose about this risk?
What happened to Israeli semiconductor operations (Intel Kiryat Gat, Tower Migdal HaEmek) during 2023-2025 conflicts, per filings?
What were the actual effects of the Russia-Ukraine war on neon and other gases?
How did Red Sea shipping disruptions (2024) affect chip-related logistics?
Did South Korea's December 2024 political crisis affect industry operations?
primary_sources: Samsung / SK hynix business reports (DART) risk sections

title: Natural-hazard risk to chip production: earthquakes, floods, drought, storms and climate exposure
why_it_matters: Chip production is concentrated in earthquake zones (Taiwan, Japan) and in places exposed to drought and storms. Past events show how long recovery takes and which products were hit.
questions: What were the production impacts and recovery times of: Taiwan 1999 Chi-Chi earthquake, 2011 Tohoku earthquake, 2011 Thailand floods (HDD/back-end), 2016 Kumamoto earthquake, 2021 Taiwan drought, 2021 Texas winter storm, 2024 Hualien earthquake, 2024 Noto earthquake, 2024 Hurricane Helene at Spruce Pine (high-purity quartz)?
How much output was lost per company disclosures, and what was insured?
What climate-exposure assessments exist for major chip clusters (water stress, heat, sea-level)?
What design and operational mitigations are used (seismic isolation, water recycling, backup power)?
primary_sources: TSMC 20-F and press releases on earthquakes (1999, 2024)
Taiwan Water Resources Agency data on 2021 drought
Samsung/NXP/Infineon statements on the 2021 Texas storm
Sibelco / The Quartz Corp statements on Spruce Pine (2024)
secondary_sources: Academic studies on 2011 disasters and supply chains

title: Operational disruption risk: fab fires, contamination, power outages, gas leaks and pandemic lockdowns
why_it_matters: Single incidents in a fab or a region have repeatedly caused global shortages (AKM 2020 fire, Renesas Naka 2021 fire, Kioxia 2022 contamination, Malaysia 2021 lockdowns). They show how thin the margin for error is.
questions: What happened, how long it lasted and what it cost for major incidents 2000-2026 (Renesas Naka fire 2021, AKM Nobeoka fire 2020, Kioxia/WD contamination 2022, Samsung Pyeongtaek/Hwaseong power outages, Taiwan grid outages 2021-22)?
How did COVID lockdowns in Malaysia (2021), Shanghai (2022) and elsewhere disrupt back-end operations?
Which products and customers were affected downstream?
What recovery playbooks were used?
primary_sources: Renesas press releases on Naka fire (2021)
Taiwan Power Company outage reports (to verify)

title: Critical-input supply risk: gases, minerals, chemicals and quartz (neon, helium, gallium, germanium, rare earths, fluorochemicals, high-purity quartz)
why_it_matters: Chipmaking depends on inputs that come from very few places: China produced about 90% of gallium [CLM-0345], Ukraine supplied much of chip-grade neon [CLM-0531], and Spruce Pine supplies high-purity quartz. Disruption risk here is high and hard to hedge.
questions: For each critical input, where is it produced and purified, what are the chip-industry uses, and what substitutes exist?
What happened in actual disruptions (neon 2022, Ga/Ge 2023-25, rare earths 2025, fluorochemicals 2019, helium shortages)?
How much buffer inventory do fabs hold, and how quickly can alternative supply be qualified?
What government stockpiles or critical-minerals programmes cover these inputs (US, EU CRMA, Japan JOGMEC)?
subquestions: Contradiction CON-0011 on Ukraine's neon share should be resolved here.
primary_sources: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025/2026 (gallium, germanium, helium, rare earths, quartz)
EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) and CRM list

title: Single-supplier chokepoint risk: consequences and mitigation where one firm supplies a critical tool, material or service
why_it_matters: Some items come from a single firm (EUV scanners, EUV mask inspection, some substrates and resins, leading-edge advanced packaging). This unit asks what would happen if one of them failed and what buyers do about it; the mapping of concentration itself belongs to the supply-chain-concentration units.
questions: For the evidenced single- or dual-source items (e.g. ASML EUV, Zeiss optics, Lasertec actinic inspection, Ajinomoto ABF film, TSMC CoWoS), what would a 6-12 month outage cause downstream?
What mitigation do buyers use (dual qualification, safety stock, co-investment, prepayments)?
Have any such suppliers had outages or near misses (e.g. the ASML Berlin fire 2022, to verify)?
What do supplier filings say about their own sub-supplier concentration?
primary_sources: ASML annual report (supplier dependence on Zeiss)
open_questions: Coordinate with supply_chain_concentration units owned by another planner; this unit covers consequences and mitigation only.

title: Cyclical and demand risk: AI capex sustainability, customer concentration and overbuild indicators
why_it_matters: Much of the 2024-2026 growth rests on a few hyperscalers' AI spending. If that slows, accelerator makers, HBM producers, advanced packaging and toolmakers would be hit together. Assessing the risk needs evidence on concentration and on past overbuild episodes.
questions: How concentrated are AI chip revenues by customer (NVIDIA, Broadcom, TSMC, SK hynix customer-concentration disclosures)?
What is hyperscaler capex and how is it financed (company filings)?
What indicators have analysts and official bodies used to judge overbuild (inventory, capex/revenue ratios, GPU rental prices)?
How does the current episode compare with 2000-01 telecom and 2018 crypto/memory reversals?
What would a memory price reversal do to 2026 growth forecasts (WSTS forecast sensitivity)?
primary_sources: IMF / BIS (Bank for International Settlements) commentary on AI investment (to verify)

title: Technology execution risk: node delays, yield failures and technology bets that failed
why_it_matters: Technology leadership has changed hands through execution failures (Intel's 10nm delay, reported yield problems at advanced nodes) and bets that did not pay (e.g. 3D XPoint/Optane, 450mm wafers). New transitions (GAA, backside power, High-NA, hybrid bonding) carry similar risk.
questions: What documented cases of node delays and yield failures exist, and what did they cost (Intel 10nm/7nm, Samsung 3nm GAA, GlobalFoundries 7nm exit 2018)?
Which technology bets were abandoned and why (450mm wafers, 3D XPoint, EUV delays pre-2019)?
What risks do companies disclose for current transitions (High-NA EUV, backside power, hybrid bonding, 300mm GaN/200mm SiC)?
How does technology risk transmit to customers (e.g. product delays)?

title: Cybersecurity, IP theft and insider risk in the semiconductor supply chain
why_it_matters: Chip designs and process know-how are among the most valuable trade secrets in the world, and fabs are complex connected systems. Malware (TSMC 2018), supplier ransomware and repeated theft cases show the risk.
questions: What cyber incidents have disrupted chip production or suppliers (TSMC 2018 malware, MKS 2023 ransomware, Nvidia 2022 breach, others) and what did they cost?
What trade-secret theft cases have been prosecuted (Micron vs UMC/Fujian Jinhua, Samsung/SK hynix engineer cases in Korea, TSMC 2nm case in Taiwan 2025, ASML cases)?
What security standards apply (SEMI E187 equipment cybersecurity, SEMI E188, Taiwan national core key technologies rules)?
What is known about hardware security risks (trojans, supply-chain tampering) relevant to trusted-foundry programmes?
primary_sources: US DOJ press releases on Micron/Fujian Jinhua (2018) and outcome (to verify)
Taiwan National Security Act amendments on core key technologies (2022)
Korea prosecutors' statements on Samsung technology leaks (to verify)

title: Regulatory enforcement and compliance risk: export-control penalties, diversion and smuggling of controlled chips
why_it_matters: Firms face large penalties when controlled items reach restricted users (e.g. a US$300m BIS penalty on Seagate in 2023, to verify), and advanced AI chips are reportedly smuggled into China through third countries. This risk shapes sales practices and compliance spending.
questions: What major export-control enforcement actions against semiconductor firms occurred 2018-2026 (BIS penalties, DOJ cases), and what were the violations?
What evidence exists on smuggling or diversion of AI chips (DOJ indictments, Singapore/Malaysia investigations, BIS guidance on red flags)?
What have Malaysia and Singapore done to tighten controls?
What compliance programmes do firms disclose?
primary_sources: BIS enforcement press releases and final orders
US DOJ press releases on chip smuggling cases (2024-2026, to verify)
Malaysia MITI Strategic Trade Act permit rules for AI chips (2025, to verify)
secondary_sources: CSET/CNAS analyses of AI chip smuggling

title: Company-failure and financial risk: bankruptcies and distressed exits in semiconductors
why_it_matters: Capital intensity and cycles repeatedly push chip firms into insolvency or distressed sale (Qimonda 2009, Elpida 2012, Tsinghua Unigroup 2021, HSMC Wuhan, Wolfspeed 2025). Failures remove capacity and strand customers and governments' investments.
questions: Which significant semiconductor insolvencies and distressed exits occurred 2008-2026, and what were the causes?
What happened to their capacity, customers and IP (acquirers, liquidations)?
How much public money was lost or restructured (e.g. Chinese local-government projects)?
What early-warning signs appeared in filings?
primary_sources: Insolvency court records and administrator reports (Qimonda Munich; Elpida Tokyo District Court, to verify)

title: Resource and environmental constraint risk: water, power, emissions and chemicals regulation for fabs
why_it_matters: Fabs use large amounts of ultra-pure water and electricity and emit greenhouse gases and PFAS. Droughts, grid limits (increasingly shared with AI data centres) and chemical bans could constrain where and how chips are made.
questions: How much water and electricity do major chipmakers use (company sustainability reports) and in which stressed basins?
What grid constraints affect chip clusters (Taiwan, Korea Yongin cluster power supply, Arizona, Japan Kyushu)?
How could EU PFAS and F-gas rules and US EPA rules affect fab chemistries and costs?
What emissions targets have chipmakers set, and what is the scope-1 contribution of process gases?
primary_sources: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK hynix sustainability reports
ECHA PFAS restriction proposal and updates
US EPA Subpart I GHG reporting for electronics manufacturing
Taiwan Power Company and Korea KEPCO planning documents (to verify)
secondary_sources: Academic papers on fab water use

title: Business continuity and resilience practices: how chip firms and buyers mitigate disruption
why_it_matters: After the shortage and repeated shocks, firms say they have changed inventory policy, multi-sourcing and continuity planning, and governments added crisis tools. Whether this has really reduced risk is the question.
questions: What changes in inventory targets, multi-sourcing and dual-fab qualification have chip firms and buyers disclosed since 2021?
What business-continuity practices do major fabs disclose (e.g. TSMC earthquake recovery, water trucking)?
What government crisis tools exist (EU Chips Act crisis toolbox, US DPA, Japan economic security act designations of semiconductors as specified critical materials)?
What evidence shows these measures worked in later disruptions (2024 Hualien, 2025 Nexperia)?
primary_sources: Japan Economic Security Promotion Act specified critical materials designations (Cabinet Office, to verify)
open_questions: prereq: Natural-hazard risk; Operational disruption risk; Geopolitical weaponisation case studies

title: Risk exposure matrix by participant type and region (synthesis)
why_it_matters: Bringing the risk units together shows which participant types carry which risks, in which regions, with what evidence. This is the input the later audit and opportunity work needs.
questions: For each participant type (ontology leaf), which risks apply, with evidence of past impact?
Which regions face compounded risk (e.g. Taiwan: conflict + earthquake + power + water)?
Where is evidence thin and interviews needed?
primary_sources: Outputs of the risk units in this batch
USITC and CRS reports on supply-chain risk (SRC-0070, SRC-0106)
open_questions: prereq: all risk units (Taiwan, weaponisation, natural hazard, operational, critical inputs, chokepoints, cyclical, technology, cyber, enforcement, company failure, resources)
